# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>

Policy: <level>

# Research Report: The Federal Reserve's G.19 Statistical Release — "Consumer Credit"

## 1. Executive Summary

The G.19 "Consumer Credit" Statistical Release is a monthly publication of the **Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System** reporting national aggregate amounts of credit outstanding that has been extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, **excluding loans secured by real estate** (i.e., mortgages and home equity lines). It is one of the Federal Reserve's oldest statistical products—the Fed has been the primary producer of aggregate consumer credit statistics **since 1942**—and it remains the authoritative public source for aggregate, non-mortgage household debt in the United States, currently tracking roughly **$5.1–5.2 trillion** in outstanding balances (as of mid-2026 data).

Your provided description is **accurate** and closely matches the Federal Reserve's own official language. A few nuances and updates are worth flagging, detailed in Section 2.

---

## 2. Verification of the Provided Description

Your description is essentially a verbatim match of the Federal Reserve's official release language, confirmed against the Board's own "About" page and the FRASER archive's bibliographic record:

| Claim in your description | Verification |
|---|---|
| Reports outstanding credit to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding real-estate-secured loans | ✅ Confirmed — this is the release's defining scope |
| Two major types: revolving and nonrevolving | ✅ Confirmed. Revolving = mostly credit card debt (plus overdraft plans, etc.); nonrevolving = closed-end loans such as auto, student (education), personal, boat, and RV loans |
| Reports selected terms of credit: interest rates on new car loans, personal loans, and credit card plans at commercial banks | ✅ Confirmed. Note the new-car loan maturities reported have changed over time (currently 60-month and 72-month; older documentation references 48-month) |
| Terms of credit for new motor vehicle loans at finance companies | ✅ Confirmed — includes rates, maturities, and average amounts financed at auto finance companies |

**Updates your description doesn't capture (because they postdate it):**
- As of **July 2025**, the "nonfinancial business" holder sector was retired and removed from the release (balances had diminished and source data were discontinued), and new credit union estimation methods were implemented.
- Since **June 2020**, the release reports **total managed receivables** (on-book plus off-book securitized balances combined) by sector, rather than separating on-book and securitized balances as distinct line items.

---

## 3. Publisher and Governance

- **Publisher:** Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Washington, D.C.). The statistics are produced by Board staff (the consumer credit statistics team within the research function); the release itself is issued through the Board's **Public Affairs Office** and posted to federalreserve.gov.
- **Cadence:** Monthly, generally on the **fifth business day of the month at 3:00 p.m. Eastern Time**, covering data about two months in arrears (e.g., an early-September release reports July data). Data for the most recent month are marked **preliminary** and subject to revision.
- **Data collection infrastructure:** Raw data are collected by the twelve regional **Federal Reserve Banks** from respondents in their Districts, edited at the Reserve Banks, and transmitted to the Board for central processing and estimation.

---

## 4. Legal Authority and Mandate

The G.19's origins are unusual and historically important—it grew out of the Fed's *regulatory* powers over consumer credit, not a generic statistical mandate:

- **Executive Order 8843 (August 9, 1941):** President Franklin D. Roosevelt, drawing on authority under the **Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917**, directed the Federal Reserve Board to regulate installment credit for consumer durable goods, on the grounds that liberal credit terms were stimulating demand for goods whose materials and production capacity were needed for national defense. The Fed implemented this through **Regulation W (Consumer Credit)**, which imposed down-payment and maturity requirements on consumer loans. Administering Regulation W required comprehensive data on who was lending to consumers and on what terms—this data apparatus is the direct ancestor of the G.19.
- **Subsequent authorities:** The Fed's consumer credit data role continued under various later acts and regulations, including temporary credit-control authorities (the 1948 Joint Resolution, the 1950 Defense Production Act, and the **Credit Control Act of 1969**, rescinded in 1982), and more durably under the Federal Reserve's general **monetary policy responsibilities** under the Federal Reserve Act—including the statutory direction (Section 2A, added by the Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977) to maintain growth of "monetary and credit aggregates."
- **Terms-of-credit collection (1972):** Began at the request of the **President's Committee on Interest and Dividends**, established as part of Phase I of President Nixon's wage-price controls program.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act compliance:** The underlying surveys are cleared by OMB under control numbers (see Section 6), which is a preservation-relevant hook—each collection has documented purposes, burdens, and periodic Federal Register renewal notices.

---

## 5. History and Evolution

### Timeline of major changes
- **1942–1952:** The Board published **three separate releases**: *Consumer Instalment Credit of Industrial Banks*, *Consumer Instalment Credit of Industrial Loan Companies*, and *Consumer Instalment Loans of the Principal Types of Financial Institutions*. These were later consolidated into the single G.19.
- **Title history (per FRASER):** "Consumer Credit (G.19)," 1942–1976 → "Consumer Instalment Credit (G.19)," 1976–1996 → "Consumer Credit," 1996–present.
- **1972:** Terms-of-credit series begin (see above).
- **1983:** Major revision after an exhaustive internal review—refocused the program on highest-priority items, dropped low-quality materials, and reduced respondent burden.
- **1989:** Consumer loans held in **pools of securitized assets** added to total consumer credit outstanding (a series break).
- **1999:** "Automobile" and "Other" credit categories combined into a single "**Nonrevolving**" category because the split lacked a suitable benchmark; the release was reformatted to add historical depth.
- **2003:** **Federal government and Sallie Mae student loans** added to total consumer credit. After Sallie Mae's privatization completed in Q4 2004, its loans moved fully into the finance company sector; the line item was renamed "Federal government" in December 2009. This change is why the G.19 today is a primary tracker of the ~$1.6 trillion federal student loan portfolio.
- **2012:** Flows (break-adjusted changes) added for all loan categories; commercial banks and savings institutions combined into the "**depository institutions**" sector (June 2012).
- **2013:** New sector "**Nonprofit and educational institutions**" added, plus memo items for **student loans and motor vehicle loans outstanding**.
- **2020 (June):** Shift to reporting **total managed receivables** (on-book + off-book) per sector.
- **2025 (July):** Nonfinancial business sector decommissioned; new credit union estimation methodology implemented (documented in Fed Notes of July 8, 2025).

### Implication for researchers
The long time series (some FRED series begin **January 1943**) contains numerous documented **series breaks**. The Fed handles this by publishing **break-adjusted flows** alongside levels, so users can compute growth rates uncontaminated by methodology or source-data changes. Anyone doing long-horizon time-series work must consult the release's revision history and the Fed's "About" documentation.

---

## 6. Content, Methodology, and Data Collection

### What's in the release (three pages)
1. **Page 1, top:** Seasonally adjusted annualized growth rates, levels, and flows for total, revolving, and nonrevolving credit (3 most recent months, 5 quarters, 5 years).
2. **Page 1, bottom:** Quarterly terms of credit (bank rates on new-car and personal loans, credit card rates; auto finance company terms).
3. **Page 2:** Not-seasonally-adjusted **levels by major holder**: depository institutions, finance companies, credit unions, federal government, nonprofit and educational institutions—plus memo items for student and motor vehicle loans.
4. **Page 3:** **Flows** by the same holders.

### Estimation methodology
- **Benchmark-and-indicator framework:** Comprehensive but lower-frequency "benchmark" data anchor the levels; higher-frequency "indicator" data estimate monthly movements between benchmarks using **proportional interpolation** (an optimization that minimizes month-to-month changes in the estimate-to-indicator ratio, subject to hitting benchmarks exactly).
- **Seasonal adjustment:** Seasonal factors estimated separately for revolving and nonrevolving credit using **X-12-ARIMA** on 10 years (120 months) of history, re-benchmarked annually before the September release; seasonally adjusted levels are built recursively from seasonally adjusted flows.
- **Break adjustment:** Flows exclude discontinuities (e.g., loan sales to out-of-scope institutions, methodology changes) so growth rates reflect real economic activity.

### Primary data sources (Fed collections, with OMB control numbers)
| Report | Form | OMB No. | Panel | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weekly Report of Selected Assets and Liabilities (commercial banks) | FR 2644 | 7100-0075 | ~850–875 banks, voluntary stratified sample | Monthly indicator for depository institutions (also feeds the H.8 release) |
| Domestic Finance Company Report of Consolidated Assets and Liabilities | FR 2248 | 7100-0005 | ~50–70 companies | Monthly estimates for finance companies |
| Quarterly Report of Interest Rates on Selected Direct Consumer Installment Loans | FR 2835 | 7100-0085 | ~75–82 banks, voluntary; "most common rate" as of the Saturday ending the first full week of Feb/May/Aug/Nov | Terms of credit: 60- and 72-month new-car loans, 24-month personal loans |
| Quarterly Report of Credit Card Interest Rates | FR 2835a | 7100-0085 | ~25 banks | Credit card rates: "all accounts" and "accounts assessed interest" |
| Quinquennial Census/Survey of Finance Companies | FR 3033p/s (FR 3303s) | 7100-0277 | Finance company universe every 5 years (most recent benchmark as of June 30, 2021) | Benchmarking and panel updates |

### Secondary sources
FFIEC **Call Reports** (FFIEC 031–034; OMB 7100-0036) — the quarterly legal filing required of all insured depositories, used to benchmark depository institution estimates; **America's Credit Unions** (formerly CUNA); the **U.S. Department of Education** (federal student loans); and additional private-sector vendors.

---

## 7. Access, Formats, and Technical Details

- **Current release:** federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/ (HTML + PDF).
- **Historical data:** HTML tables of levels and flows by type and holder, plus an archive of past release PDFs; full release dates calendar published in advance.
- **Data Download Program (DDP):** Preformatted CSV packages (Consumer Credit Outstanding SA/NSA, Terms of Credit, Major Holders, Revolving, Nonrevolving, Flows) and a complete **SDMX-ML XML** file (~6 MB zipped). ⚠️ **Important transition:** The Board announced (July 2026) that the DDP's "Build Your Package" feature is being removed (week of November 9, 2026) in preparation for the **eventual retirement of the DDP entirely**. Users are being directed to **FRED** (see below) and release-page XML downloads. This is a material event for anyone with automated pipelines hitting the DDP.
- **FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis):** All G.19 series available (release ID 14), with API access, graphing, and a formal DDP–FRED partnership ensuring continuity. Flagship series include **TOTALSL** (Total Consumer Credit Owned and Securitized, monthly, SA, from January 1943). Units note: series switched from billions to millions of dollars in 2025 — a wrinkle for long automated series pulls.
- **ALFRED:** Vintage ("real-time") versions of G.19 series, with vintages available from December 1996 forward — essential for revision-sensitive research, since the Board's own site carries only currently-published (fully revised) data.
- **FRASER (St. Louis Fed digital library):** Scanned historical releases, 1976–present, with full bibliographic metadata (including alternate titles) — the authoritative archival record of the release as a *document*.
- **Citation:** Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, G.19 Consumer Credit Statistical Release; FRED provides suggested series-level citations.
- **Cost/licensing:** Free; federal government work, widely redistributable with attribution (FRED notes some graph-content caveats).

---

## 8. Typical Users

- **Federal Reserve policymakers and staff:** The G.19 feeds directly into monetary policy analysis of household sector conditions and the consumer credit channel; it complements the Z.1 Financial Accounts and H.8 bank balance sheet releases.
- **Financial market participants and economic forecasters:** The monthly release is a scheduled, market-watched indicator of consumer borrowing and spending momentum (a rough proxy for consumer durables demand and credit conditions).
- **Academic and policy researchers:** Studying household leverage, credit cycles, securitization, the growth of federal student lending, and financial crises (the 2008–09 contraction in revolving credit and the student-loan-driven divergence are canonical G.19 stories).
- **Consumer advocates and policy activists:** Tracking credit card debt levels and interest rates (the "accounts assessed interest" series is a widely cited measure of what revolving borrowers actually pay), auto loan costs, and the federal student loan portfolio — all directly relevant to CFPB policy debates, state usury/fee legislation, and student debt policy.
- **Journalists and the public:** Monthly coverage of "consumer credit rose/fell" headlines derives from the G.19.
- **Data librarians and instructors:** Frequently used as a teaching dataset (long history, clean access via FRED API, well-documented methodology).

---

## 9. Benefits to the Public

1. **Transparency into household financial health:** It is the only comprehensive, public, monthly aggregate measure of non-mortgage consumer debt in the U.S., letting citizens, journalists, and policymakers see how much Americans owe on credit cards, auto loans, and student loans.
2. **Accountability for the federal student loan portfolio:** The "Federal government" holder line (~$1.6 trillion) makes the scale of federal student lending visible in a standard statistical product.
3. **Price transparency in consumer credit markets:** The terms-of-credit series provide benchmark interest rates for auto loans, personal loans, and credit cards, supporting comparison shopping, regulatory analysis, and research on the pass-through of monetary policy to consumer borrowing costs.
4. **Macroeconomic stabilization:** By informing Federal Reserve policy with timely credit data, the series indirectly supports the statutory goals of maximum employment and stable prices.
5. **Scientific infrastructure:** Decades of consistent, documented, freely downloadable data (with vintages in ALFRED and scanned originals in FRASER) make it a model public statistical asset for reproducible research.

---

## 10. Limitations and Caveats (Important for Data Scientists and Activists)

- **Excludes mortgages and all real-estate-secured debt** — by design. For total household debt including mortgages, use the **FRBNY Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit** (credit-bureau-based) or the Z.1 Financial Accounts. The G.19 and FRBNY reports measure overlapping but differently-sourced populations and frequently diverge in levels and trends.
- **Aggregate only:** National totals; no geographic, demographic, income, or distributional breakdowns. It cannot answer questions about *who* holds the debt (use the Survey of Consumer Finances or FRBNY/Equifax data for that).
- **Estimation, not enumeration:** Monthly figures are model-based estimates benchmarked quarterly/quinquennially; recent months are preliminary and revised, sometimes substantially.
- **Series breaks:** Securitization (1989), student loan inclusion (2003), sector consolidations (2012), managed-receivables switch (2020), and sector removals (2025) all create discontinuities. Use break-adjusted flows for growth rates.
- **Terms-of-credit quirks:** Bank rate surveys are voluntary, small-panel (~25–82 respondents), "most common rate" measures, neither benchmarked nor seasonally adjusted.
- **Deliberate scope decisions can lag the market:** E.g., nonfinancial business balances were dropped only in 2025 after source data withered; rapidly evolving lender types (fintechs, BNPL) have historically been under-covered until source data catch up — a documented, acknowledged challenge the Fed addresses via periodic methodology notes.

---

## 11. Preservation and Archival Landscape (For Preservationists and Data Librarians)

- **Multi-institution redundancy:** The dataset is actively mirrored across the Federal Reserve Board (current + historical HTML/CSV/SDMX), the **St. Louis Fed** (FRED/ALFRED, which the Board now designates as the succession path for the DDP), and **FRASER** (document-level scans back to 1976, plus predecessor publications).
- **Active risk — DDP retirement:** The Board's Data Download Program is being wound down (BYP feature removed November 2026; full retirement planned). Preservationists should **snapshot DDP packages and SDMX files now**, and note that FRED is the official continuity path but presents data as currently revised.
- **Vintage preservation:** Only ALFRED systematically preserves historical vintages (from 1996). Pre-1996 "as first published" numbers survive mainly in the scanned releases on FRASER and in older Fed bulletins — valuable for revision studies.
- **Format migration notes:** Unit changes (billions → millions, 2025) and repeated restructuring of tables/sectors mean archived CSVs from different eras are **not naively concatenable**; metadata (series keys, sector definitions at time of publication) must be preserved alongside data.
- **Documentation to preserve with the data:** The release "About"/methodology pages, technical Q&A, Fed Notes on methodology changes (2024 revolving credit note; 2025 credit union and nonfinancial business notes), annual performance evaluations, and OMB clearance packages (which document the statutory basis and design of each underlying collection).
- **Records context:** As a continuing federal statistical release produced under OMB-cleared collections, both the releases and the underlying survey documentation fall within federal records frameworks; FRASER functions as the de facto public archive of record for the historical series.

---

## 12. Related and Complementary Datasets

- **Z.1 Financial Accounts of the United States** (Fed) — household sector balance sheets, consumer credit memo items.
- **H.8 Assets and Liabilities of Commercial Banks** (Fed) — source indicator data.
- **G.20 Finance Companies** (Fed) — companion release from the same FR 2248 collection.
- **FRBNY Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit** — includes mortgages; microdata-based.
- **Survey of Consumer Finances** (Fed, triennial) — distributional detail.
- **Household Debt Service and Financial Obligations Ratios** (Fed; the FOR series is discontinued).
- **CFPB Consumer Credit Trends** and credit card market reports — regulator perspectives on the same markets.

---

## 13. Key URLs

| Resource | URL |
|---|---|
| Current release | federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/ |
| About/methodology | federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/about.htm |
| Data description & technical Q&A | federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/g19_data_description.htm |
| Historical data | federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/hist/ |
| Data Download Program | federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=G19 |
| FRED release page | fred.stlouisfed.org/release?rid=14 |
| Flagship FRED series (TOTALSL) | fred.stlouisfed.org/series/TOTALSL |
| ALFRED vintages | alfred.stlouisfed.org/series?seid=TOTALSL |
| FRASER archive (documents) | fraser.stlouisfed.org/title/g19-consumer-credit-75 |

---

### Bottom line
Your description is verified as accurate against the Federal Reserve's own language. The G.19 is an 80-plus-year-old statistical institution born from wartime credit controls (EO 8843, Regulation W), maintained today under the Fed's monetary policy mandate and OMB-cleared survey programs, published monthly by the Board of Governors, and serving policymakers, markets, researchers, journalists, and consumer advocates. The most time-sensitive fact for any data steward is the **announced retirement of the Board's Data Download Program**, with FRED designated as the succession platform and FRASER/ALFRED as the historical and vintage archives of record.

- **Moderate Risk:** Two minor items worth noting: (1) a September 2025 correction to DDP flows series (a bug fix republished within one day; PDF/HTML/historical tables unaffected — a correction, not a removal); (2) the nonfinancial business sector ceased being reported in July 2025, but its historical series remain published in archived releases and FRED. Neither constitutes removal of historical data.
- **No Known Issue:** Full historical archive intact across four redundant platforms (Board, FRED, ALFRED, FRASER). The one forward-looking concern is the announced retirement of the Data Download Program (BYP feature removed November 2026; full DDP retirement planned), but FRED is the officially designated succession platform and the underlying release files remain on federalreserve.gov.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** All historical data remain accessible with no known alterations. Preservationists should nonetheless snapshot DDP packages before the platform retires, as a matter of prudent practice rather than demonstrated loss.

## Category 2: Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- **Gone:** No evidence — collection and publication are fully active.
- **High Risk:** No statutory publication deadline has been missed (the G.19 has no statutory deadline at all); no collection or publication has been skipped; no ICR is expired. The Fed's self-funding meant its statistical releases **continued on schedule through the 2025 federal government shutdown**, unlike BLS/Census products.
- **Moderate Risk:** No delays found. The release calendar shows publication on the fifth business day every month through 2025–2026 (January–June 2026 marked "Updated"/published; July–December 2026 scheduled, with September 8 and October 7, 2026 releases confirmed published).
- **No Known Issue:** ICRs are active and being renewed before expiration through the Board's OMB-delegated PRA authority: FR 2644 extended for three years effective April 2025 (90 FR 13863); FR 2835/2835a extended for three years in April 2024 (89 FR 23018); FR 2248 three-year extension proposed July 2026 (91 FR, comment period through September 8, 2026) with revisions effective June 2027 — a routine renewal, not a lapse; FR 3033 quinquennial census extension in process since January 2026.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** Publication is on time, monthly, with active ICRs renewed ahead of expiration — and the Fed's independent funding insulates it from appropriations lapses that halted other statistical agencies.

## Category 3: Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- **Gone / High Risk (reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency):** One real, but narrow, granularity reduction occurred: beginning with the July 8, 2025 release, the **nonfinancial business holder sector was removed** — driven by greatly diminished balances and discontinuation of U.S. Census Bureau source data, not by budget or policy cuts. Frequency (monthly) and timeliness (fifth business day) are fully maintained, and the FR 2248 renewal proposes burden reduction and clarity improvements without cutting content feeding the core G.19 series.
- **Moderate Risk:** The sector removal is a genuine (if peripheral) reduction, and the announced **system-wide 10% staff reduction** plus ongoing reliance on voluntary small panels (FR 2835a: ~25 banks) represent emerging risks to future granularity if staff or respondent attrition deepens. The 2025 change also demonstrates the dataset's vulnerability to upstream source-data discontinuation (Census data).
- **No Known Issue:** Arguable for the core series: total/revolving/nonrevolving levels and flows, major holders, and terms-of-credit series are all maintained, and 2024–2025 saw documented methodological **improvements** (new credit union estimates, revolving credit estimation notes).

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** A data element (one holder sector) was actually removed in 2025, and announced workforce reductions create an emerging risk — but timeliness, frequency, and all core series remain intact, with recent methodology changes on net improving the estimates.

---

## Category 4: Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- **High Risk (vague authorization / substitutes / no programmatic use):** Partially applicable. The G.19 is **not explicitly required by statute**. Its original authority (Executive Order 8843/Regulation W, Credit Control Act of 1969) lapsed decades ago. Partial substitutes exist: the FRBNY Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit and the Z.1 Financial Accounts.
- **Moderate Risk:** The release has a **clear, continuous programmatic use**: Section 2A of the Federal Reserve Act directs the Fed to maintain growth of "monetary **and credit aggregates**," and the G.19 is the Board's primary monthly consumer credit aggregate, a documented input to monetary policymaking (stated explicitly in the FR 2835 supporting statement) and to the Z.1. The substitutes are not true substitutes — the FRBNY report is quarterly, credit-bureau-based, and differently scoped; the Z.1 is quarterly and partly derived from the G.19's inputs. This matches the rubric's Moderate definition: not explicitly statutorily required, but required for implementation of a federal program, without full substitutes.
- **No Known Issue:** Not applicable — there is no statute naming this collection.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** The lack of an explicit statutory mandate and the existence of adjacent (though incomplete) alternative collections mean continuation rests on institutional practice and the Fed's general credit-aggregates mandate rather than hard legal requirement.

## Category 5: Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- **Gone / High Risk:** Not met for the statistics function. There is **no evidence of targeted cuts to the Board's research/statistics divisions or termination of funding**; the Fed is self-funded through interest on its securities portfolio and is not subject to congressional appropriations. However: Vice Chair Bowman's announced ~30% cut to the Supervision & Regulation Division (500 → ~350 staff) exceeds the 40%/1,000-staff thresholds *within that division*; there was a sustained campaign against Fed leadership (Trump threats to fire Powell, the attempted removal of Governor Lisa Cook, and a DOJ criminal investigation of Powell — the latter ended April 2026). "Leadership removed" has not occurred, but leadership pressure was severe and chair transition to Kevin Warsh (nominated January 2026) is underway.
- **Moderate Risk:** Squarely met. In May 2025, Chair Powell announced a plan to **reduce Federal Reserve System headcount ~10% (~2,400 of 24,000 positions) over several years**, via attrition and a deferred resignation program; the Reserve Banks also aligned with the January 2025 federal hiring freeze. This lands in the rubric's 10–39% band, and the leadership turmoil ("threatened change in leadership") is well documented.
- **No Known Issue:** Not met — a 10% cut is announced and leadership change is actively contested, though no change in the chair had been effected as of this writing.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** A system-wide 10% staff reduction is underway, and leadership has been under direct political attack (DOJ probe, removal attempts, chair transition). Mitigating: self-funding, attrition-based implementation, no evidence statistics divisions are specifically targeted, and the G.19's low marginal cost and small survey panels make it comparatively resilient.

---

## Category 6: Policy

**Evidence:**
- **Gone / High Risk:** Not met. None of the G.19's ICRs is a Presidential Action-driven collection; there is **no negative policy note** on the release pages; and the administration's documented pressure campaign against the Fed has targeted **interest-rate policy and personnel, not statistical products**. No Fed statistical release has been altered to conform to administration priorities.
- **Moderate Risk:** The administration has made repeated statements suggesting institutional changes at the Fed (rate pressure, renovation scrutiny, nominee Warsh's stated interest in shaking up staffing — "'dead wood'"), and Fed staff reductions were explicitly framed as aligning with the President's government-downsizing effort. But none of these statements targets the G.19 or its inputs.
- **No Known Issue:** The only post-January 2025 change affecting what is published — the July 2025 nonfinancial business sector removal — was announced April 7, 2025, methodology-driven (Census source data discontinuation), and processed through normal public notice, not administration priorities. All other activity (ICR renewals, DDP-to-FRED migration planning, methodology notes) is routine or quality-improving.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** No notable administration-priority-driven changes to what data is collected or published. The Fed's institutional independence — fiercely litigated and publicly defended through 2025–2026 — has so far shielded its statistical output even amid extraordinary political pressure on its leadership.

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Level |
|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Future Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Data Quality | **Moderate Risk** |
| Statutory Context | **Moderate Risk** |
| Staffing and Funding | **Moderate Risk** |
| Policy | **No Known Issue** |

**Overall assessment:** The G.19 is among the more resilient federal statistical products — self-funded, shutdown-proof, on-schedule, actively renewed under OMB clearances, and redundantly archived across the Board, FRED, ALFRED, and FRASER. Its principal vulnerabilities are structural rather than acute: no explicit statutory mandate, a demonstrated (if minor) 2025 reduction in scope, dependence on discontinued third-party source data, and an announced 10% system-wide workforce reduction unfolding amid unprecedented political pressure on Federal Reserve leadership. Prudent preservation action now — archiving DDP packages, SDMX files, and methodology documentation before the DDP retires — would secure the record at low cost.
